findings.finding: The plan claims 'Deriving `fallback_on` from `ResolutionClass` rather than an independent tuple means the two classifications cannot drift' — but `FallbackModel(fallback_on=...)` accepts a tuple of EXCEPTION TYPES, not ResolutionClass values. The existing `_map()`/`_map_http()` functions classify an exception into a ResolutionClass; they have no inversion that produces a set of exception types from a class. In practice the implementer must still enumerate exception types manually (the very drift problem the plan claims to avoid). The 'derived from ResolutionClass' mechanism does not exist as described.
findings.location: Approach section — '5. `fallback_on` reuses the EXISTING failure taxonomy'; AC 'the chosen `fallback_on` condition is documented in-code with the SDK-retry caveat'
findings.suggested_fix: Add a `fallback_exception_types() -> tuple[type[BaseException], ...]` function to `failure.py` that returns the exception types corresponding to the 'provider-switch helps' classes (httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ConnectTimeout, httpx.TimeoutException, ModelHTTPError with 429/529/5xx status, ModelAPIError). Pass its output as `fallback_on=fallback_exception_types()` at FallbackModel construction. This is the inversion that makes drift prevention real rather than asserted.

findings.finding: The plan mandates capability intersection over all candidates (decision 4), but the existing call site `capabilities_for(model)` at runner.py:365 reads `.profile` off a single model object. A `FallbackModel` wrapper does not expose a `.profile` attribute, so it will fall through to the conservative-record path (the warning branch in `capabilities_for`) rather than computing the intersection. The plan does not specify how to bridge the intersection semantics to the current `capabilities_for` interface.
findings.location: Approach section — 'DECIDED 4. Capabilities are the CONSERVATIVE INTERSECTION'; runner.py:365 `caps = capabilities_for(resolved if self._model_override is not None else model)`
findings.suggested_fix: Compute `caps` from the candidate list BEFORE constructing `FallbackModel`: call `capabilities_for` on each `FallbackTarget`'s resolved string/object and intersect the resulting `ModelCapabilities` fields (AND for booleans, most-restrictive string for `prompt_cache_style`). Store the intersected `caps` and pass it — not the `FallbackModel` object — to `cache_settings_for` and `provenance_for`. This is purely additive and leaves the existing `capabilities_for` interface intact.

findings.finding: The plan states `provider_provenance` will record `ran_model` 'resolved AFTER the call from the model that answered', but does not specify the mechanism by which the runner extracts which candidate inside a `FallbackModel` actually executed the call. pydantic-ai's `FallbackModel` has no documented post-call introspection API in the installed environment, and no such property appears in the codebase.
findings.location: Approach section — 'DECIDED 4. Provenance records BOTH the candidate set and what actually ran'; AC '`provider_provenance` records the ordered `candidates` AND a `ran_model` equal to the model that actually answered'

findings.finding: `FallbackModel` exposes no public API to identify which sub-model answered a given call — `FallbackModel.model_name` returns a combined identifier string, not the individual model that ran. The plan's AC asserts `ran_model` is 'resolved AFTER the call from the model that answered' but names no mechanism; GitHub issue #3028 shows this was explicitly requested as a missing feature.

findings.suggested_fix: Inspect `ModelResponse.model_name` on the response returned by `FallbackModel.request()` — pydantic-ai sub-models set this on their own responses, so it should carry the answering model's name. Confirm this in a spike test before writing the AC. If it does not hold, each fallback entry may need a thin `WrapperModel` that stamps a known tag on each response.

findings.finding: The plan asserts that `ran_model` (which fallback sub-model actually answered) is 'resolved AFTER the call from the model that answered', but names no pydantic-ai API surface on FallbackModel that exposes this. findings.finding: The plan states `capabilities_for`, `cache_settings_for`, and `_check_tool_capability` will be computed as a conservative intersection over primary + every fallback, but `capabilities_for()` today dispatches on a model object's `.profile` or a `provider:model` string. A `FallbackModel` object's own `.profile` attribute (if any) is unspecified by the plan, and the intersection algorithm is not described — it is unclear whether the plan calls `capabilities_for` N times on sub-model strings/objects or relies on a FallbackModel-level `.profile`.

The extraction mechanism is a referenced but undefined processing rule.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Merge or clearly differentiate the two `fallback_on` AC items: either combine them into one criterion that checks BOTH the error-code boundary AND the callable-not-tuple structure, or explicitly label them as 'behavior test' and 'structural/type test' so it is unambiguous that two distinct tests are required.

'a test asserts `fallback_on` is given a CALLABLE predicate and that the predicate returns True for a 429/529/5xx and for a transport error, and False for 401/403 and for a 400 context-length error — exercised through `failure.py`'s classifier, not a hardcoded type tuple'
Both items enumerate the same four error codes and the same True/False boundary.
findings.finding: Two AC items test the same `fallback_on` error-code boundary (429/529/5xx fires; 401/403 and 400 does not fire) with the same inputs, differing only in framing (one says 'fires/does not fire', the other says 'callable predicate returns True/False'). This creates ambiguity: are two separate tests required, or one? An implementer may write two overlapping tests or, conversely, treat one as redundant and skip it.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — items: 'a test asserts `fallback_on` fires on a 429/529/5xx...' and 'a test asserts `fallback_on` is given a CALLABLE predicate...'
scenarios: Implementer writes two nearly-identical tests with no additional coverage, or treats one as redundant and skips it, leaving the 'callable not tuple' structural check unverified.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace both items with a single AC: 'a test asserts `fallback_on` is a CALLABLE predicate (not a type tuple) that, when exercised through `failure.py`'s classifier, returns True for 429/529/5xx and transport errors and False for 401/403 and 400 context-length errors.' Then add a separate integration-framed item only if you want to test the FallbackModel's response to those error codes end-to-end.
